extracted.intended_audience: theologians, clergy, and educated lay readers interested in Anglican/sacramental theology and doctrinal history
extracted.subtask_description: A close, scholarly critique of doctrines concerning baptism, regeneration, the Eucharist, apostolic succession, and justification within Anglican and broader Christian theology. The page evaluates historical interpretations (Fathers, Reformers, Council of Trent) and assesses their coherence with Scripture, reason, and pastoral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical abstractions that override moral/spiritual reality
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that 'regeneration, which precedes a moral one in time' has been put into a series of inferences and is supported principally by reliance on the general enlightenment of the early Church writers. Insisting upon shadows as if they were realities, and requiring men to accept as a religious verity of prime importance a dogma that is the offspring of false metaphysics, must be a [injury] to the interests of religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrines should not substitute metaphysical subtleties for concrete moral and spiritual realities; when a conception weakens love and pursuit of truth or produces disunion and distrust among Christians it is practically injurious. Evaluate doctrines by their moral and spiritual consequences as well as by their speculative pedigree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not define the Spirit's presence as an inert lodgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine insisted on by some is that 'at the moment of baptism, the soul receives the Holy Spirit... remains within the soul, even if the baptized, as soon as he becomes capable of moral acts, be faithless and wicked, until it is expelled... by an indefinite amount of wickedness.' This is said to be 'intolerable... in its moral and spiritual aspects' and to evacuate the Scriptural phrase 'Christ in us' of its meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid doctrines that imagine the Holy Spirit as a passive, permanently lodged entity independent of the moral life of the person. The presence of the Spirit must be tied to moral effect and spiritual fruit; doctrines that make the Spirit a mere ontological fact in a soul irrespective of moral response are criticised as harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define spiritual presence by operation/effect, not mere spatial relation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A spiritual being is not in a spiritual [thing] as a material thing is in a material thing; it is in it, or present to it, inasmuch as it acts upon it... the heart itself which, by the power of the Spirit, must bear the fruit of virtue, — not a something lodged in it, as the seed in the ground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'presence' of the Holy Spirit (or similar spiritual realities) in terms of activity and effects on the heart and life rather than as a static indwelling comparable to physical containment. Evaluate claims of presence by their observable spiritual effects and moral fruits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simplistic momentary-substantiation models of regeneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common fallacies about momentary Rubstantiation: (1) because we are passive in creation we are passive in spiritual re-creation; (2) because a seed may be latent and later germinate, so a spiritual gift poured into a child's soul may remain latent until reason awakens it. These analogies are misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume regeneration is a purely instantaneous, passive impartation that merely awaits future moral manifestation. Consider regeneration as having aspects that may be gradual in manifestation and requiring the co-operation (or response) of the human faculty; beware literal analogies with physical generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand sacraments as spiritual agencies producing effects in the receiver
rubrics_metrics.description: The sacrament is not for the bread and wine but for the soul of the receiver; 'the presence in the Eucharist is a spiritual presence or agency for the production of spiritual effects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Eucharistic presence primarily as an operative spiritual reality aimed at nourishing the receiver's soul, not as a claim that the material elements themselves are rendered holy or converted in substance. Evaluate Eucharistic doctrines by how they account for spiritual nourishment and practical devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not separate the voice of God from reason in doctrinal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Replies such as 'We must not reason a priori on these matters, but receive what the voice of God has declared' are criticized: 'Alas! that thus separate the voice of God from reason and the inward Holy of [God] which God has given us as an inward Holy of [conscience].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that scriptural claims and ecclesiastical pronouncements be tested by reason and internal consistency; avoid appeals that shut down rational evaluation. Reason and Scripture should be in dialogue when assessing doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anachronistic readings of the Church Fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading ancient writers like Irenaeus or Tertullian, one must not modernize them: 'Waterland's interpretation of Irenaeus... is, in my opinion, a perfect anachronism; it imputes him modern immaterializing views, quite alien from the general frame of his mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret patristic texts in their historical and intellectual context; do not project modern metaphysical distinctions onto ancient authors. Evaluate patristic evidence carefully, noting genre, historical concerns, and differing metaphysical assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the plain man's notion of substance when interpreting doctrinal language
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Article concerning the change of substance of bread and wine, Mr. Ward's claim that it 'speaks popularly' and thus conflicts not with Roman metaphysic is criticized: 'the plain man means not the mere qualities of bread... he means the bread itself, with all that belongs to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing doctrinal formulations, do not assume the framers were metaphysically naive; ordinary language about 'substance' carries an intuitive kernel that should not be dismissed as merely 'popular' phraseology. Be cautious in arguing that historical articles were intentionally non-metaphysical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat apostolic succession as an outward means preserving visible Church identity, not magical transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Episcopal succession is described as 'a fixed outward means by which the identity of the visible Church... is preserved' and as 'a leading symbol of permanent visibility,' but the author warns against rendering it a physical continuity that conveys spiritual powers like 'a stream of electricity along a metal wire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand succession as an institutional and symbolic continuity that aids preservation of doctrine and order; avoid doctrines that reduce succession to a literal, physical transmission of identical spiritual authority or spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame justification doctrines to preserve Christ as the efficient cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Though there are Tridentine, Anglican (Bull), and Lutheran renderings of St. Paul's 'justification by faith,' all parties agree 'that Christ is the efficient cause, in His sacrifice, the meritorious cause of salvation.' The dispute is not about salvation itself but about the internal principle (what in us links us to redemption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formulating doctrines of justification, ensure that Christ's central and sole meritorious role is preserved; debates should focus on the instrumental/internal connection (faith, holiness, works) without denying Christ's primacy. Avoid turning the dispute into disagreement about whether Christ saves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in asserting good works simultaneously as gift and merit without clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Canons of Trent affirm 'the good works of the justified are both gifts of God and merits of the justified person himself' — a formulation the author finds potentially incoherent or at least in need of clarification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid doctrinal formulations that create apparent contradictions (e.g., calling good works both pure gifts and merits) without explanatory nuance. Clarify the sense in which works are gifts from God and how they function relative to merit, grace, and reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presumptuous schemes of hierarchical attainability of holiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The author criticizes the notion taught in some schools that 'a man can do more in the way of good works and saintliness than another is bound to do... that there is a kind and degree of holiness which some men may and ought to seek and obtain, which the generality of the faithful cannot attain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal systems should not promote presumptuous hierarchies of sanctity that imply certain Christians are capable of attainments inaccessible to others; maintain humility and universality in teachings about holiness and reward.
